title: An actor in a play
hook: you're an actor in a play someone else wrote; your job is to play the part well (Enchiridion 17)

segments.voice: Yesterday: beside the weeping. Your line was with them, steady. When someone brought you their trouble, could you be warm and grounded at once? Day three hundred forty-nine.

Every school play has the kid who wanted to be the lead and got cast as the third tree from the left. Some of those kids sulk through every rehearsal. And every so often, one of them decides to be the best third tree the school has ever seen. Swaying in the wind on cue. Rustling at the sad part. Parents talk about that tree for years. Nobody chose their role, and the play didn't care. What they did with it was theirs. Epictetus took the theater, the great public art of his world, and made it one of his sharpest pictures of a life. Today: an actor in a play.
screen: `THE THIRD TREE FROM THE LEFT.` → `SULK, OR SWAY ON CUE.` → `AN ACTOR IN A PLAY.`

segments.voice: First, the picture. Remember, Epictetus says in section seventeen, that you are an actor in a play, and the play is as the author wants it. If short, then short. If long, then long. Second, the parts. If the author wants you to play a poor man, play even that one well. Or someone lame, or an official, or a private citizen. He lists them flatly, beggar and governor side by side, as if they were just costumes. Third, the line that splits the work. Your business, he says, is to play the given part well. Choosing the part belongs to another. Who is the author? Epictetus usually speaks of God or Zeus, ordering the whole. Some modern readers hear it as nature, or circumstance, or simply the hand you were dealt. Either way, the split is the same. Casting isn't yours. Acting is. Fourth, the word. The Greek for actor was hypokrites. English took it over and it slid into hypocrite: someone acting a part that isn't true. Epictetus means the opposite. Play your part truly, with your whole self. Centuries later Shakespeare wrote: "All the world's a stage, And all the men and women merely players". Epictetus would add one thing: merely, maybe, but the playing is everything you get to do. Parent, patient, new hire, caregiver, the one who stayed home this year. If someone hands you the third tree, sway like you mean it.
screen: `THE PLAY IS AS THE AUTHOR WANTS.` · `A POOR MAN, A RULER, PLAY IT WELL.` · `CASTING ISN'T YOURS; ACTING IS.` · `HYPOKRITES: THE ACTOR.` · then, large: `PLAY THE PART WELL.`

segments.voice: Name today's part, plainly, the way a program would list it. Maybe: tired parent. New employee. Patient in a waiting room. Friend who has to say something hard. Don't judge whether it's a good part. Just name it. Then picture one scene ahead of you today, and see yourself playing it well: the tone of voice, the small gesture, the line delivered kindly. Breathe, and step into the role. The bell holds the time.
An actor in a play. Epictetus' picture of a life: the part is given, short or long, rich or poor; your work is to play it well. Today's word.
screen: `AN ACTOR IN A PLAY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: play the part well. Whatever role today hands you, even the third tree, give it your best performance. Day three hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism think of their circumstances as a role they didn't choose, and put their effort into playing it well.

original.note: Greek, Enchiridion 17: an actor; the root of English hypocrite.

trapdoor: what you thought: fake it till you make it.
what it means: you didn't choose your part, but you can play it well and truly.
what a scholar hears: hypokrites, actor; the Stoic Ariston and the Cynic Bion used the stage image before Epictetus, and Marcus returns to it at the end of the Meditations.

notes: Enchiridion 17 paraphrased (actor in a drama as the author/teacher wishes; short or long; poor man, lame man, magistrate, private person; 'to play well the part given; to choose it belongs to another'). Confirm.
As You Like It 2.7: 'All the world's a stage, / And all the men and women merely players' — confirm wording (modernized spelling).
Trapdoor: Ariston of Chios and Bion of Borysthenes as earlier users of the actor image (Diogenes Laertius 7.160; Teles); Marcus 12.36 ends with the actor dismissed by the director. Confirm or soften.
'Epictetus usually speaks of God or Zeus': confirm phrasing; the modern readings are presented without ranking.
